newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. hopes Pyongyang finally serious on peace talk.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hopes Pyongyang finally serious on peace talk.

text.p: U.S. officials Tuesday were cautious about North Korea's agreement to join four-party peace talks, expressing hope the announced plan for negotiations next month finally represents serious engagement by Pyongyang.
"We're very pleased with this agreement (for talks to open in New York on August 5) and we look forward to having this go forward," Deputy U.S. National Security Adviser James Steinberg said.
But he noted that getting the Stalinist North to the bargaining table had been a lengthy process with many false starts.

The announcement hours earlier in New York that the United States, China, South Korea and North Korea would meet on August 5 to make procedural decisions for negotiations "is an important step," Steinberg told reporters.

"But we take it one step at a time because it's been something that we've recognised all along ...is (a) difficult road to go forward and we hope finally this will represent a serious engagement on the four-party process," said Steinberg, in Hong Kong with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright for the transfer of the territory from Britain to Chinese control.
During a meeting in New York in April, Pyongyang agreed in principle to the talks, which are intended to replace the fraying armistice from the 1950-53 Korean War with a peace treaty.
But threatened by famine and with its economy in ruins, North Korea linked its participation to a specific commitment on food aid and an end to U.S. trade sanctions.

Washington and Seoul refused to meet these demands as a condition of Pyongyang coming to the table. But they have made clear that these issues will be discussed as part of the peace negotiations and indicated that, as part of that process, North Korea could expect to see these concerns met.

In announcing the agreement in New York, senior diplomats from Washington, Seoul and Pyongyang said the August 5 talks would discuss and decide procedural matters for the plenary session, including the earliest agreeable date, venue and agenda.
The negotiations were first proposed by President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam in April 1996.
